question.text:
Which of the following sets are orthogonal?

  1. ${U}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \right\}$
  2. ${V}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \right\}$
  3. ${W}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -3 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} \right\}$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of the given sets as $\{\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2\},$ $\{\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2 \},$ and $\{\mathbf{w}_1,\mathbf{w}_2,\mathbf{w}_3\},$ respectively.

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthogonal if the following conditions on each set hold:

  • $\mathbf{u}_1\cdot\mathbf{u}_2=0.$

  • $\mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_2=0.$

  • $\mathbf{w}_1\cdot\mathbf{w}_2=0,\quad\mathbf{w}_1\cdot\mathbf{w}_3=0,\quad\mathbf{w}_2\cdot\mathbf{w}_3=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

  • For the set $U,$ notice that \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_1\cdot\mathbf{u}_2&=\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}\cdot\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}= 10 - 9 - 1 = 0 & {\color{green}\checkmark}\\ \end{align*} So, the set ${U}$ is orthogonal.

  • For the set $V,$ notice that \begin{align*} \mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_2&=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\cdot\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}= 4 - 4 + 4 = 4 \neq 0 &{\color{red}\times} \end{align*} So, ${V}$ is not an orthogonal set.

  • For the set $W,$ notice that \begin{align*} \mathbf{w}_1\cdot\mathbf{w}_2&=\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\cdot\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -3 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}= 10 - 9 - 1 = 0 & {\color{green}\checkmark}\\[3pt] \mathbf{w}_1\cdot\mathbf{w}_3&=\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\cdot\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}= 0 + 3 - 3 = 0 & {\color{green}\checkmark}\\[3pt] \mathbf{w}_2\cdot\mathbf{w}_3&=\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -3 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}\cdot\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}= 0 - 3 + 3 = 0 & {\color{green}\checkmark} \end{align*} So, the set ${W}$ is orthogonal.

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "$U$ and $W$ only".

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthonormal if the following conditions on each set hold:

  • $\mathbf{u}_1\cdot\mathbf{u}_2=0 \quad \text{and}\quad \begin{cases} \mathbf{u}_1\cdot\mathbf{u}_1=1 \\ \mathbf{u}_2\cdot\mathbf{u}_2=1. \end{cases}$

  • $\mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_2=0 \quad \text{and}\quad \begin{cases} \mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_1=1 \\ \mathbf{v}_2\cdot\mathbf{v}_2=1 . \end{cases}$

  • For the set $V,$ notice that \begin{align*} \mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_2&=\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\cdot\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ -1 \end{bmatrix}= -1-1 = -2 \neq 0 & {\color{red}\times} \end{align*} So, ${V}$ is not an orthonormal set.

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to row echelon form, as follows:

\begin{align*} M&= \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 0 & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & 0 \\ -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{14}} & \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{14}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{14}} & 0 \end{array}\right] &&\begin{array}{l} R_1 := \sqrt{10}\cdot R_1 \\ R_2 := \sqrt{14}\cdot R_2 \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 0& -1 & 3 & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 1& 0 \end{array}\right] &&\begin{array}{l} R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2 \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -2& 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 3& 0 \end{array}\right] \end{align*}

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get $x_2=3x_3.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

\[ -2x_1+3(3x_3)+x_3 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x_1=5x_3. \]

So, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 5x_3 \\ 3x_3 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_3 \in\mathbb{R}. \]

Setting $x_3=1,$ we obtain the vector $ \mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$

Now, we need to normalize $\mathbf{x}.$ Notice that $\| \mathbf{x} \| = \sqrt{5^2+3^2+1^2} = \sqrt{35}.$ So, we normalize $\mathbf x$ as follows:

\[ \dfrac{\mathbf{x}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|}=\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{35}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{35}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{35}} \end{bmatrix} \]

Therefore, an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ is \[ \left\{\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{14}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{14}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{14}} \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{35}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{35}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{35}} \end{bmatrix} \right\}. \]

Finally, $|x_1|+|x_2|+|x_3|= \left|\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{35}}\right| + \left|\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{35}}\right| + \left|\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{35}}\right| = \dfrac{9}{\sqrt{35}}.$

question.text: Consider the orthonormal set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $\mathbf x = [x_1,\,x_2]^T,$ extend the set so that it forms an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ What is the value of $|x_1|+|x_2|?$ \[ {U}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \right\} \]
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vector of ${U}$ as $\mathbf{u}_1.$ To extend the given set to an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$, we need to find a second vector $\mathbf{x}$ such that $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ and

\[ \mathbf{u}_1\cdot\mathbf{x} = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}x_1+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}x_2 = 0 . \]

From the above equation, we get $x_1=-\dfrac1 2x_2.$

So, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac 1 2x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in\mathbb{R}. \]

Setting $x_2=-2,$ we obtain the vector $ \mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}.$

Now, we need to normalize $\mathbf{x}.$ Notice that $\| \mathbf{x} \| = \sqrt{1^2+(-2)^2} = \sqrt{5}.$ So, we normalize $\mathbf x$ as follows:

\[ \dfrac{\mathbf{x}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|}=\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is \[ \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \right\}. \]

Finally, $|x_1|+|x_2|= \left|\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right| + \left|-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\right| = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{5}}.$

question.explanation:
Let's denote the vector of ${U}$ as $\mathbf{u}_1.$ To extend the given set to an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$, we need to find a second vector $\mathbf{x}$ such that $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ and

\[ \mathbf{u}_1\cdot\mathbf{x} = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{3}{5}x_1+\dfrac{4}{5}x_2 = 0 . \]

From the above equation, we get $x_1=-\dfrac4 3x_2.$

So, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac 4 3x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in\mathbb{R}. \]

Setting $x_2=-3,$ we obtain the vector $ \mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}.$

Now, we need to normalize $\mathbf{x}.$ Notice that $\| \mathbf{x} \| = \sqrt{4^2+(-3)^2} = 5.$ So, we normalize $\mathbf x$ as follows:

\[ \dfrac{\mathbf{x}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|}=\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{4}{5} \\ -\dfrac{3}{5} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is \[ \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{3}{5} \\ \dfrac{4}{5} \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{4}{5} \\ -\dfrac{3}{5} \end{bmatrix} \right\}. \]

Finally, $|x_1|+|x_2|= \left|\dfrac{4}{5}\right| + \left|-\dfrac{3}{5}\right| = \dfrac{7}{5}.$

example.title: Extending a Set to Form an Orthonormal Basis

question.text: Consider the orthonormal set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $\mathbf x = [x_1,\,x_2,\,x_3]^T,$ extend the set so that it forms an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^3.$ What is the value of $|x_1|+|x_2|+|x_3|?$ \[ {U}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \end{bmatrix}\right\} \]
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of ${U}$ as $\mathbf{u}_1,\, \mathbf{u}_2.$ To extend the given set to an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$, we need to find a third vector $\mathbf{x}$ such that $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ and

\[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{u}_1\cdot\mathbf{x} = 0 \\ \mathbf{u}_2\cdot\mathbf{x} = 0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}x_1+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}x_3 = 0 \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}x_1+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}x_2+\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{6}}x_3 = 0. \end{cases} \]

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to row echelon form, as follows:

\begin{align*} M&= \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & 0 \end{array}\right] &&\begin{array}{l} R_1 := \sqrt 5\cdot R_1 \\ R_2 := \sqrt{6}\cdot R_2 \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 2& 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 2& 0 \end{array}\right] &&\begin{array}{l} R_2 := R_2+\dfrac{1}{2}R_1 \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 2& 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & \dfrac{5}{2}& 0 \end{array}\right] \end{align*}

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get $x_2=-\dfrac{5}{2}x_3,$ and from the first equation, we obtain $x_1=-\dfrac{1}{2}x_3.$

So, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{2}x_3 \\ -\dfrac{5}{2}x_3 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_3 \in\mathbb{R}. \]

Setting $x_3=2,$ we obtain the vector $ \mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ -5 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$

Now, we need to normalize $\mathbf{x}.$ Notice that $\| \mathbf{x} \| = \sqrt{(-1)^2+(-5)^2+2^2} = \sqrt{30}.$ So, we normalize $\mathbf x$ as follows:

\[ \dfrac{\mathbf{x}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|}=\begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{30}} \\ -\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \end{bmatrix} \]

Therefore, an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ is \[ \left\{\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{30}} \\ -\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \end{bmatrix} \right\}. \]

Finally, $|x_1|+|x_2|+|x_3|= \left|-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{30}}\right| + \left|-\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\right| + \left|\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{30}}\right| = \dfrac{8}{\sqrt{30}}.$

question.text: Consider the orthonormal set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $\mathbf x = [x_1,\,x_2]^T,$ extend the set so that it forms an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ What is the value of $|x_1|+|x_2|?$ \[ {U}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix} \right\} \]
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vector of ${U}$ as $\mathbf{u}_1.$ To extend the given set to an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$, we need to find a second vector $\mathbf{x}$ such that $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ and

\[ \mathbf{u}_1\cdot\mathbf{x} = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}x_1-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}}x_2 = 0 . \]

From the above equation, we get $x_1=\dfrac{2}{3}x_2.$

So, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{3}x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in\mathbb{R}. \]

Setting $x_2=3,$ we obtain the vector $ \mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}.$

Now, we need to normalize $\mathbf{x}.$ Notice that $\| \mathbf{x} \| = \sqrt{2^2+3^2} = \sqrt{13}.$ So, we normalize $\mathbf x$ as follows:

\[ \dfrac{\mathbf{x}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|}=\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is \[ \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix} \right\}. \]

Finally, $|x_1|+|x_2|= \left|\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\right| + \left|\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\right| = \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{13}}.$
